1:
All take the passage of Christ, and one turns that into an argument about the chapter before. Adam Clarke observes that Jews and Christians agree the first seven verses belong to him, and reasons that since they continue the prophecy of the chapter before, that prophecy cannot belong to Cyrus. John Calvin gives the reason for the abruptness: the prophets, when they promise something hard to believe, bring in Christ at once, since in him all promises are ratified; the deliverance from Babylon was the foretaste of a redemption including the full restoration of the Church. He is careful about the title. The name servant belongs to all the godly, and peculiarly to teachers, but here marks a work with nothing in common with any other; it belongs to the human nature, the divine being eternal and equal in glory to the Father; and it was assumed voluntarily, so nothing was detracted from his rank—a point the ancient writers covered by the word dispensation. Charles Ellicott reads it as pointing neither to the visible nor the ideal Israel but to One who is the centre of both, and calls elect another word by which this prophet fashioned Christian theology.

The verb rendered uphold is disputed. Clarke gives, on whom I lean, after the custom of kings leaning on a beloved servant. Calvin sets out both possibilities without choosing: taken passively it means God will lean on his Anointed so as to lay the whole charge upon him, as masters do with faithful servants, and taken actively, I will raise him up, or exalt him, or support him in his rank. He objects to neither. Matthew Henry reports the same alternative in passing—my servant on whom I lean, so some read it—while keeping the received rendering, and lists five things the words say of the Father: he owns him as employed, chose him rather than let him thrust himself forward, put confidence in him, bore him up, and delighted in him. On the last word Clarke shows how wide the term for judgment is, covering rule, order and plan, the rule of right and of religion, and every stage of a legal process from trial to acquittal; here, he says, it means the law to be published by the Messiah. Ellicott takes it in the narrower sense of law or ordinance and marks the change from an earlier chapter, where the Temple was the centre from which such knowledge flowed and here the servant’s own teaching is.

The quietness of the second verse is variously explained. Keil and Delitzsch make it a contrast with rival teachers: though certain of his calling and bringing the highest and best, his manner is quiet and humble, the opposite of lying teachers who exalted themselves by noisy demonstration—he brings what commends itself and needs no forced trumpeting. Ellicott sets the same picture against false prophets who might rave as in an orgiastic frenzy, recalls a Greek lawgiver who affected a soothsayer’s inspiration to draw attention, and distinguishes the places named: the street is the open space where men harangued the people, the gate being kept for the formal administration of justice. Calvin gives three reasons for the silence—that we may form no earthly conception of him, that knowing his kindness we may hasten to meet him, and that our faith may not languish though his condition be mean—and notes that he forbade publishing the miracles. Henry says the same in his own idiom: it was never to be proclaimed lo here or lo there, as when great princes ride in progress, his kingdom being spiritual and its weapons not carnal. John Gill supplies a different sense for the second verb: it may mean not lifting up the voice but lifting up faces, that is, accepting persons, which is how one old version takes it. John Wesley reads the crying as contention or vainglory.
3:
The two figures are handled tenderly, then guarded. Keil and Delitzsch define them exactly—the reed cracked and half-broken already, the wick burning feebly and nearly out—and report an early Latin father who made the bruised reed the faith of Israel and the glimmering wick the momentary zeal of the Gentiles; they answer that the words hardly admit the distinction, the reference being general, to those whose life hangs by a slender thread. They find more in the negative than it says: he will not merely refrain from destroying the life that is dying out, he will save it, his course being not to destroy but to save. Charles Ellicott draws the same inference from the rhetoric, that the simple he shall not break implies the opposite extreme, the care that props and supports; but he adds a limit from the parable of the lamps that go out, which not even he could light again unless the bearers bought oil for themselves. John Gill identifies the weak as young converts, reckoned worthless before God, as nothing by men, and unworthy by themselves, weak especially in faith and having little hope—though their love, he says, is the strongest thing in them.

John Calvin praises the same mildness and at once refuses to let it be misused. Lest anyone suppose such forbearance encourages vice, he insists vices must be corrected without flattery, and marks out who the gentleness is for. It does not suit those who obstinately resist, nor the fierce and headstrong, who deserve no such treatment but must be broken and crushed as by the strokes of a hammer, by the severity of the word; it belongs to those who, amid many deficiencies, have integrity of mind, or in whom some good beginning may be seen. We must guard against both extremes, neither crushing the weak by severity nor encouraging evil by smooth language. He finds the token of the meekness in the dove at the baptism, and asks the ministers of the gospel to show the same, not extinguishing the feeblest sparks but kindling them.

The verbs of the fourth verse are disputed. Keil and Delitzsch observe that both point back to the figures just used, and on that ground reject a derivation taking the second from a root meaning to run and giving, he will not be rash or impetuous but execute his calling with wise moderation; it must come from the root meaning to break. Ellicott notices the same echo and draws a warmer conclusion, that in helping others to strength and light the servants of the Lord, after the pattern of the Servant, gain light and strength for themselves. Adam Clarke reports that a rabbi cites the passage with an extra word, his force, not in the present Hebrew text but seemingly needed to make the sense plainer—and admits he had put it into his own translation before he met the remark. Gill notes the first verb may mean to grow dim, like a lamp for want of oil, which is why one old version turns the clause round and reads, he shall shine. Ellicott adds that the Greek rendering of the last line, quoted in the Gospel as, in his name shall the Gentiles hope, is a paraphrase rather than a translation. Calvin illustrates the danger of the wrong mildness with a story of two preachers in a populous city, one reproving vices boldly and one courting the people. The flatterer, expounding a prophet, lighted on a consoling passage and declaimed against harsh reprovers who terrify men with thunderbolts of words; but next day the prophet changed his subject and rebuked the wicked sharply, and the wretched man had to retract before hearers whose memories were fresh, making himself abhorred by good and bad alike. John Wesley keeps the plain sense, that the isles are countries remote from Judea, which will gladly receive the doctrine.
5:
The pile of divine titles before the commission is explained as needed, not ornamental. John Calvin says the promise might be thought incredible, especially when the outward aspect of things runs directly contrary, so the prophet brings forward proofs of the power of God—who made all things out of nothing, spread the heavens, produced vegetation, gave life to animals, and upholds everything—that our faith may rest on the word rather than on appearances. He adds a textual note without deciding it, that the first title is rendered by some powerful and by others God, and that it matters little since the meaning is the same. Matthew Henry reads them as marking God the fountain of being in three worlds: above, since he stretched out the heavens and keeps the vast expanse still upon the stretch; below, in the earth and what comes out of it; and among men, to whom he gives not only air to breathe but the breath of life and organs to breathe with, and beyond that the faculties of a rational soul. Henry finds a purpose in prefixing this to the commission, that redemption was to maintain the honour of the Creator and restore man to the allegiance he owes. Keil and Delitzsch note that the words now address the servant himself, so that by the infinite might of the caller he may be sure he will never lack power to execute his call. Charles Ellicott observes that such an accumulation of attributes to heighten a revelation has both an earlier and a later parallel in the prophets.

Who is called, and in what, is disputed. John Gill sets aside two Jewish readings, one making the called person the prophet himself and another the people of Israel, and keeps the Messiah; he then offers three renderings of the phrase in righteousness—that the call was made in a righteous manner, with the full consent of the one called; that it means unto righteousness, to bring in an everlasting righteousness; or with righteousness, since the one called came as a righteous person. Calvin rejects the second of these before it is offered. It is generally thought, he says, that the phrase points out the end of the calling, that Christ was sent to establish justice among men; but he passes by that ingenious distinction, remarking that the text does not say he shall be called to righteousness. He takes the word adverbially, as righteously, and infers the calling is lawful and therefore firm and lasting, since what is not done properly cannot endure. The word, he concludes, denotes stability, as if it had said faithfully.

The covenant itself raises two further questions. Adam Clarke reports manuscripts reading not of the people but of the age to come, the everlasting covenant, which he says gives a clearer sense; and he argues the noun should not be rendered covenant at all but covenant sacrifice, a meaning it often bears and bears undoubtedly here. Ellicott takes the opposite view, holding that the context limits the people to Israel, and makes the servant not merely the mediator of the covenant but the covenant itself, the meeting-point between God and man, just as elsewhere he is the peace and not only the peacemaker. John Wesley refuses the limitation outright, glossing the people as all people, not only Jews but Gentiles. Calvin raises the historical objection himself and answers it: why should Christ be appointed to a covenant ratified two thousand years before, when Abraham was adopted? Because that covenant had its foundation in Christ and was ratified only in the seed of Abraham, so that though made long before it was confirmed and actually sanctioned by his coming. Keil and Delitzsch add that God pledges his own name and honour to the work, since he who bears that name cannot allow the honour due him to be permanently transferred to sham gods.
7:
The opening of blind eyes is read spiritually by all, and one feels the irony. Charles Ellicott remarks that the prophet must have felt the contrast between this commission and his own, which had been to make eyes blind, and calls the prison that of the selfishness and sin which keep men from being free. Adam Clarke reads the verse as setting forth the spiritual redemption under images borrowed from the temporal deliverance, and reports a conjunction added before the last clause by three ancient versions and several manuscripts. John Calvin makes a point about who is being addressed. The words are spoken to Christ, but believers are in the prophet’s eye throughout; God is not instructing Christ what to do, as though he needed teaching, but speaking for our sake, that we may know why the Father sent him. Under these metaphors, he adds, the condition of men before that coming is declared—wretched, empty, and overwhelmed by innumerable distresses. John Gill applies the blindness to the idolatrous Gentiles, who did not know the wretchedness of their case.

The divine name draws two very different notes. Clarke observes that this is the name of four letters written in half a dozen ways, that the Jews never pronounce it, and that the true pronunciation is utterly unknown. Gill reports a variant giving a different word for the name, and adds that this is one of the names of God among the Jews, as a like word is among the Turks to this day, meaning in Arabic simply him. Calvin knows the same reading and rejects it: the word is sometimes taken as a substantive and made a proper name of God, but he explains it more simply as meaning that this is my own name and cannot lawfully be given to another. He then turns the verse into an argument about assurance. Infer from this, he says, what the disease of unbelief is, since the Lord can hardly satisfy himself with any words to express its cure; we are prone by nature to distrust and do not believe God when he speaks until he subdues our stubbornness. What follows he calls a remarkable passage: the glory of God is chiefly visible in his fulfilment of what he has promised, so that in refusing to give his glory to another he undertakes to abide by his word. John Wesley defines the name shortly, of one who has all being in and of himself.

The former and the new things are identified differently. Keil and Delitzsch take the first as the rise of Cyrus and the agitation of the nations it caused, the new things as the restoration of Israel and the conversion of the heathen; and they decline in passing to settle whether the captivity was the prophet’s historical or only his ideal standpoint. Gill looks further back and makes the former things the whole chain of fulfilled prediction—what was said to Abraham about the affliction of his posterity, what was foretold by Moses and Joshua, and lately the captivity of the ten tribes, come to pass in the prophet’s own generation. Calvin builds on experience: God speaks as if to say he had spoken so often to their fathers and been found true in everything, and that they still cannot trust him about the future, past transactions producing no effect on them. He then supplies a test for genuine prediction, drawn from plants which put forth buds and flowers before the fruit appears: God does not foretell what has already begun to happen and shrewd men might conjecture, but speaks before anything has occurred from which a conjecture could be formed. On that mark he distinguishes God from the idols, whose responses were false or ambiguous, so that those who relied on them were shamefully deceived—and where the event did seem to correspond, he says, it only plunged them deeper.
10:
How wide the summons reaches is disputed, and one dispute runs into an emendation. Adam Clarke objects that the phrase about those who go down to the sea does not suit this place and consists ill with what follows, since navigators are too confined an idea for the prophet, who means the sea at large and with it the distant nations and the dwellers on the coasts. He suspects a copyist had a familiar psalm running in his head and wrote one Hebrew phrase where another stood, which would give, let the sea roar or exult—then declines to act on his own conjecture, saying that as it differs so much from the present reading he will not take the liberty of putting it into his translation. He reports a second conjecture, unsupported by the versions. Charles Ellicott works the other way, from the one definite name in the passage. Kedar is the only touch of localisation, and starting from it the other terms gain a defined sense: the proclamation is addressed to the eastern rather than the western world, the ships are those trading down the eastern gulf, the rock is the ancient city of that name, and the islands the far coasts of the Indian Ocean. He adds that the opening words are familiar in the Psalms and probably quoted.

John Calvin refuses that precision. Kedar and the tents mean Arabia, he grants, but by a figure in which a part stands for the whole, so the whole east is meant and from the rising of the sun to its setting these praises will be heard; and the word for wilderness covers not only the tract between Judea and Arabia but the more distant countries, which people name from whatever part adjoins them, as some call mountainous the plains beyond the mountains. His annotator presses this into a rule of reading: if the sea, the islands, the deserts, the mountains, the towns and the camps are not all parts of one great picture, it is impossible to frame one, and it is absurd to take the first and last widely as hyperbole while taking what lies between strictly. Keil and Delitzsch say only that the new things furnish both the impulse and the materials of a song such as the heathen world had never heard.

Clarke also uses the passage to attack a way of preaching it. He identifies the places soberly—the desert and the rocky country as the two divisions of Arabia, the mountains probably the famous ones there, Kedar a clan dwelling mostly in tents—and quotes a traveller distinguishing the Arabs who wander with their herds, those who never abide within walls and are counted most noble, and those who live in cities. Then he turns on those who make the rock Christ, its inhabitants true believers and the singing their rejoicing in salvation, and says they abuse and disgrace both the passage and the pulpit. He recalls a clergyman who spent an hour proving from these words that the rock was Christ under four heads, as foundation, strength, refreshment and place of prospect—and delivers his verdict, that all of it is true in itself but false of the words it was built on, which have no such meaning. Calvin is severe in a different direction: the new song means an excellent and elegant song, not an ordinary one, and the more favours received the louder the praise ought to be; but it cannot be sung except by renewed men, since it must proceed from the deepest feeling of the heart. He adds that to be lukewarm, or to mutter, or to sing to oneself is impossible for anyone who has tasted the grace of God. John Gill and John Wesley keep the plain application, that the song is for redemption and the calling of the Gentiles, the islands meaning the remotest parts of the world.
13:
Matthew Henry declines to settle what these verses are: it comes all to one, he says, whether we make them the song the Gentile world is to sing or a prophecy of what will make way for the singing of it. On the going forth he reads the preaching of the gospel, the apostles’ ministry being their warfare, and notices that the promise to prevail against enemies may mean prevailing to make them friends. John Calvin explains the metaphor rather than the reference: God seemed concealed while he let his people be afflicted without any appearance of aid, so that to go forth means to come forth publicly to give assistance. The burning indignation and the warrior’s rush, he adds, are drawn from human feelings and accommodated to our capacity, since nothing else would make a sufficiently powerful impression. Charles Ellicott calls the image boldly anthropomorphic and says it prepares the way for a more awful picture later in the book. John Wesley supplies two comparisons, the lion over his prey and soldiers beginning a battle.

The long silence and the cry that ends it are handled with unusual care. Adam Clarke reports that the copy behind the old Greek version had an extra word here, turning the clause into a question—shall I always keep silence?—which he thinks dropped out by a transcriber’s mistake, the neighbouring word being so like it; and compares a Latin satirist’s complaint about being always a hearer only. Ellicott dates the silence to the exile, which to those enduring it seemed endless, and renders the last clause quite differently from everyone else: not I will destroy and devour, but I pant and gasp, the verbs expressing strong emotion, the cries of the travailing woman rather than any destructive act. Calvin dwells on the figure and guards it twice over. God compares himself to a mother who singularly loves the child she brought forth with extreme pain; and though it may be thought such things are not applicable to God, in no other way can his ardent love be expressed, since he loves more fully and perfectly than men do and nothing disorderly belongs to him. Then, because that comparison might somewhat lower the majesty of God, Calvin observes that the prophet at once adds a different feeling—as to love God resembles a mother, as to power a lion or a giant. He also finds a promise in the image itself, that the redemption would be a kind of birth, the grave serving the people for a womb.

Whether the mountains and rivers stand for anything divides the last verse sharply. John Gill reads them as kingdoms great and small, kings and governors, and applies them to the emperors who set themselves against the gospel. Ellicott agrees the description is symbolic, taking the rivers and pools for the kingdoms of the two great rivers, and adds that through what looks like purely destructive work mercy and truth are working, the literal melting into the spiritual as in a dissolving view. Calvin refuses the method outright. There is no necessity, he says, for ingenious speculations, as some have done who by an allegorical interpretation pronounce that mountains and hills mean cities and their inhabitants; the plain meaning is that no army whatsoever can resist God when he wishes to deliver his people, his power not being limited to natural means but breaking through every obstruction. Keil and Delitzsch notice a formal feature instead, a fresh example of the prophet’s habit of returning at the close of a period to the word it began with, and read the divine panting as an almighty fiery breath which turns the land of captivity into desert and clears the road home. Clarke proposes changing one letter to read not islands but dry deserts, a conjecture he thinks very probable, and Wesley glosses the hills as the most lofty and flourishing enemies.
16:
Who the blind are is not agreed. John Wesley makes them the Gentiles, led by a way of truth hitherto hidden from them, while John Gill reports a Jewish reading applying the verse to Israel. Keil and Delitzsch define them by condition rather than nation: those deprived of sight by their own sin and its punishment, the unknown ways being the ways of deliverance known to God alone, the dark space their state of hopeless misery, the rugged places the dangers that met them on every side in a foreign land. John Calvin presses the figure further and turns it into an advantage. The blind are those whose affairs are so intricate and disordered that they do not know which way to turn, and see nothing but deep gulfs on every hand; and it is often good for us, he says, to have no way open, to be hemmed in and even blinded, so that we learn to depend solely on God—for so long as a plank is left that we think we can seize, we turn to it with our whole heart. It is better, he concludes, to be blind men guided by the hand of God than by excessive sagacity to build labyrinths for ourselves; though the promise, he adds, is to believers alone, not to the worldly wise who wish to see in spite of him.

Adam Clarke spends his space on the grammar of the last clause, and on where it leads. He notes a variant for the word rendered paths, in three versions and nine manuscripts, then examines the verb translated will I do unto them. As written it is a second person, thou wilt do; the traditional pointing makes it first, but the letter that would settle it is missing here and present in forty manuscripts, and the Jewish authorities agree a past form stands for a future. He then observes that the pronoun does duty for a phrase with a preposition, so that I have done them means I have done for them—and remarks that this same ellipsis, applied lately to a famous passage, has cleared a difficulty that puzzled expositors for two thousand years, produced dissertations without number, and set the learned quarrelling over whether Jephthah sacrificed his daughter, both parties being ignorant alike of the place and of the terms of the vow.

The shame of the idolaters closes the section, and they divide over how literally to take the charge. Charles Ellicott reads it historically, as a section winding up, the victories of Cyrus bringing confusion on the worshippers of idols he was to overthrow. Keil and Delitzsch keep it general, saying the acts of judgment and salvation unmask the false gods to their worshippers’ utter confusion, and that as the false religions fall the redemption of Israel becomes at the same moment the redemption of the heathen; they mark this as the end of the prophecy’s first half, joined to what follows by the phrase about leading the blind. Calvin anticipates an objection. Were men so stupid, he asks, as to say to an image, thou art my god? For all superstitious persons confessed that God is in heaven and did not openly ascribe divinity to wood or stone. His answer is that they ascribe the power of God to images all the same, since in fleeing to statues and making vows to them they give away what belongs to God alone; so it is vain to cloak their ignorance under plausible excuses, and the prophet neither exaggerates nor falsely accuses them. Even had they never said the words, he adds, their madness would appear in their supposing they cannot reach God’s ear without bowing before an image. Gill offers the turning back both ways, either as conversion from idols to the living God or as the flight of those not converted, seeking rocks and mountains to hide them.
18:
The summons to the deaf and blind raises an objection, and two of them answer it. Matthew Henry says there is no absurdity in commanding what we are not of ourselves sufficient for, since men have powers they might employ better,, and compares the man with the withered hand: he could not stretch it out, yet had he not attempted it he would not have been healed, and the healing was owing not to his act but to divine power. John Gill makes the point by distinguishing the senses: the summons asks men to use the outward hearing and sight they have, within the compass of natural men, to attain the spiritual hearing they lack. John Calvin notes that the two words are not used here as a few verses earlier: there they described men overwhelmed by affliction and blinded by sorrow, here men who shut their eyes in the midst of light. He then widens the charge: though the reproach falls directly on the Jews he would rather say it condemns all men, since it applies also to the Gentiles, on whose consciences God had impressed the knowledge of himself. Gill reports a Jewish reading taking the address to Israel, and prefers the impenitent Gentiles; Charles Ellicott takes those addressed as ideally the servant of the Lord, in whom the personal Servant’s pattern should have been reproduced.

The next verse is contested at almost every word. Calvin reports an interpretation making it the retort of wicked men against the prophets—whom do you call blind? take that to yourself—and rejects it, since what follows explains the blindness in terms that cannot apply to prophets. He rejects a second reading, which refers the word rendered perfect to Isaiah or to Christ and has one of them accused of blindness. His own account descends from all mankind to the Jews and then to the priests, on whom the heaviest blame lies, since the nearer we come to God the less excusable we are. Adam Clarke proposes two changes. The clause about the messenger should read, as he to whom I have sent my messengers, which he says only two old versions render rightly; and in the last clause blind should be deaf—the mistake palpable, the correction self-evident and admissible, he adds, even had there been no authority for it. On the disputed word Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree against the received rendering. Both refuse perfect; Keil and Delitzsch also refuse a proposal making it the purchased one and settle on one allied to God in friendship, his confidant; Ellicott gives the devoted or surrendered one, notes its kinship with the modern words for a Muslim and for Islam,.

Clarke has the sharpest note on the last verse. The received text carries one form of the verb, corrected by the Masoretes in the margin and now standing in a hundred and seven manuscripts and five editions; he supposes this was the reading of most manuscripts in their day, which out of some superstition they would not admit into their standard text, and adds that these critics saw a fault without knowing where it lay or how to mend it, though it was plain to a judicious eye. Keil and Delitzsch note the alternation of thou and he and observe that the marginal reading makes the two halves uniform. Ellicott takes the verse of the actual Israel and refuses one application outright, saying the transfer of the words to the sufferings of Christ is scarcely tenable. Calvin makes the blindness double and warns our guilt will be double if we shut our eyes when the light is shown and our ears when the word is taught. Henry says it more simply: multitudes are ruined for want of observing what they cannot but see, perishing not through ignorance but mere carelessness. John Wesley reads the messengers as the priests and teachers appointed to instruct.
21:
The verse about God being well pleased is read three ways. John Calvin says it is interpreted variously—some giving, the Lord hath so willed it, others, he is merciful—and settles on, the Lord is willing, meaning inclined to deliver his people, so as to magnify his law and display his righteousness. Charles Ellicott changes the tenses: the Lord was well pleased, and made his law great and glorious. That had been his purpose, and he had not failed in it. John Wesley supplies a motive of his own: God waits for repentance not for the people’s sake but for the glory of his own faithfulness, and will not be forward to destroy those who profess the true religion, lest his law be exposed to contempt. Adam Clarke notes that where the received text has law the old Greek read praise, giving, he hath exalted his own praise.

Which captivity is meant is the next question, and Ellicott admits he cannot easily settle it. It is hard to say, he writes, whether the prophet contemplates the exiles in Babylon or sees far off another exile after a second and more fatal falling away; the tone of despondency comes in strangely after so glorious a promise, and on the whole he prefers the second. He returns to it at the close, judging that the burning heat of wrath and the violence of war—his rendering of the last verse—fit wars and rumours of wars better than the long equable continuance of the exile. John Gill has no such hesitation and refers it all to the Roman siege, when nation, city and temple were ruined together. Clarke reads one verb as a plural passive, on the authority of two scholars, so the line gives, all their chosen youths are taken in the toils; and at the next verse he reports two old versions reading they have sinned where the Hebrew has we have sinned. Ellicott adds that the holes are rock-caves, used here not as refuges but as dungeons.

On why the calamity came they agree, and press it differently. Calvin says the people are miserable through their own fault, rejecting a God who would otherwise have done them good and setting aside every remedy, as men past hope will do; and he turns the accusation on his readers, that if we see the Church in a ruinous condition we ought to ascribe it to our own iniquities, by which we do not suffer God to do us good. He names the difficulty exactly: everybody acknowledges God the author of all things, but ask whether adverse events are his chastisements and men will be ashamed to confess it, there being nothing they are persuaded of with more difficulty. The Jews of that day, he says, thought their sufferings came by chance, or that they lacked their fathers’ strength, and so kept their minds on external causes. Keil and Delitzsch say that when they ceased to be deaf to this crying contradiction they would own the punishment merited. Ellicott adds that the wrath, aiming at restoration, is only another aspect of the same love. Calvin reads the question of the twenty-third verse as asking who, subdued at last by affliction, repents even though late, and draws from it the use of all threatening: God does not punish as though he delighted in vengeance, but that we may be on our guard for the time to come. On the closing image Calvin reads the poured-out wrath as a thunderbolt or a bursting flood, and treats the war as metaphorical too, though he does not object if the enemies God raised up are meant. Clarke draws men in a burning house, scorched and still not seeing their danger, and complains that such people are approached with flattery where they should be convinced. John Wesley ends where the verse does: they were secure and stupid under the judgments.
